narrative:
The model estimated a 68% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, it judged failure more likely than success, and that prediction is why your law school application was denied.

The strongest reason was your third-year class-rank decile: at 1.00, you were far below the average among accepted students, about 5.79, and this was the single most influential factor pushing the prediction toward bar-exam failure. Your first-year class-rank decile was the second most important factor. At 1.00 versus an accepted-student average of about 6.00, it also pushed strongly toward failure. Together, these academic-position signals carried more weight than anything else.

Your upper-middle family income was the third most important factor. It was a mild factor pushing toward passing, and it is common among accepted students, at 45.4%, but it was not strong enough to offset the academic-rank concerns.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening the academic evidence most tied to bar readiness. Seek advising about why your class rank was low, consider whether additional coursework or a structured bar-preparation plan can demonstrate improvement, and discuss retaking the LSAT if a higher score is realistic. Reapply only after building a clearer record of academic progress, and include context that explains your earlier performance.
